property_summary: For every input, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer passed in constructor), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for at least some inputs, so owner()'s return must equal the deployer address for all fuzzed callers — the mutant breaks this.

For every caller and input, the reference contract's owner() returns the deployer address (the stored owner) while the mutant returns address(0), so asserting owner() == deployer for all fuzzed callers distinguishes them.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() getter returns the stored owner address (the deployer passed in constructor); the mutant returns address(0) instead, so owner() == deployer holds for all inputs on the reference but is false for some inputs on the mutant.

For every caller, C.owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer); the mutant returns address(0) instead, so the property owner() == deployer holds universally for the reference but is falsified by the mutant for some callers.

For every caller and input, the deployed contract's owner() getter returns the stored owner address (the deployer passed in constructor); the mutant that forces owner() to return address(0) will cause owner() != deployer for some fuzzed caller inputs, so asserting owner() == deployer for all fuzzed inputs holds on the reference and is violated by the mutant.

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner must always leave owner() equal to newOwner when newOwner != address(0); the mutant that allows transferring to the zero address breaks this by permitting owner() == address(0) after transferOwnership when newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must succeed (not revert) and afterward owner() equals newOwner whenever newOwner is a non-zero address; the mutant that removes the non-zero requirement allows transferring to address(0) which makes owner()==address(0) possible and thus violates the rule when newOwner==address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must succeed (not revert) and afterwards owner() equals newOwner for every non-zero newOwner; the mutant that removes the require allows transferring ownership to the zero address, making owner() == address(0) possible (violating the rule for newOwner == address(0)).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must not change owner() to address(0) when newOwner is non-zero; the mutant that removes the require allows owner() to become address(0) when newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) should return (not revert) and afterwards owner() equals newOwner when newOwner is NON-ZERO; the mutant that removes the require allows owner() to become address(0) when newOwner == address(0), so there exists an input (newOwner == address(0)) where the mutant's postcondition differs.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership with the same address should succeed (be a no-op) in the reference; the mutant rejects such no-op transfers (reverts), so there exists an input (newOwner == owner) where the mutant reverts but the reference does not.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) should succeed (not revert); the mutant adds a check that reverts when newOwner == owner(), so it breaks this rule for inputs where newOwner equals the current owner.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never reverts (the reference allows no-op transfers to the same owner); the mutant introduces a require that makes transferOwnership revert when newOwner == owner(), so there exist inputs (newOwner == current owner) where the mutant reverts but the reference does not.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) does not revert in the reference implementation (it allows transferring ownership to the same current owner as a no-op), whereas the mutant adds a require that makes transferOwnership revert when newOwner == owner(), so there exist inputs (newOwner equal to current owner) where the mutant reverts but the reference does not.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert); the mutant adds a require that makes the call revert when newOwner == owner(), so the mutant will revert for inputs where newOwner equals the current owner while the reference does not.

For any owner-supplied address x, calling setOperator(x) updates the contract's operator state to x (so c.operator() == x); the mutant that only emits the event breaks this by leaving operator unchanged for some x.

For any address newOp passed to setOperator by the owner, the reference contract updates its operator to newOp (c.operator() == newOp) while the mutant that only emits an event can leave operator unchanged for some newOp values.

For any address newOp passed by the owner to setOperator, the reference contract updates its operator() to that address; the mutant that only emits an event can leave operator() unchanged for some newOp, so there exists a fuzz input where c.operator() != newOp after calling setOperator from the owner.

For any address newOp supplied by the owner, calling setOperator(newOp) results in the contract's operator() getter returning newOp afterwards; the mutant that only emits an event (and does not assign) violates this for some fuzzed newOp values.

For any address newOp and when called by the owner, calling setOperator(newOp) always updates the public operator() getter to newOp in the correct contract; the mutant that only emits the event but does not assign will leave operator() unchanged for some fuzzed newOp, so there exists inputs where c.operator() differs after the call.

For any input address _operator, calling setOperator(_operator) results in c.operator() equaling the supplied _operator; the mutant instead sets operator to zero address for some inputs, violating this property.
For any caller who is the owner, calling setOperator(addr) sets C.operator() equal to the provided addr; the mutant instead sometimes sets operator to address(0) (breaking that equality).
After any successful owner call to setOperator(x), the contract's operator getter returns x; the mutant instead sets operator to address(0) for some inputs, breaking this equality.

For every owner-supplied address _operator, calling setOperator(_operator) results in c.operator() equaling the supplied _operator; the mutant instead assigns operator = address(0) so for some fuzzed _operator the post-call getter differs (breaking equality).

For any address a called by the owner via setOperator(a), the contract's operator getter returns a after the call; the mutant instead sets operator to address(0) causing the post-call operator() to differ for some fuzzed a.

For any caller (owner) and any address argument _operator passed to setOperator, the correct contract will set operator to the provided _operator; the mutant sets operator to msg.sender instead and thus for some fuzzed _operator (not equal to owner/caller) the stored operator will differ from the argument.

After any call to setOperator by the owner with a fuzzed address argument x, the reference contract stores operator == x (sets operator to the provided argument); the mutant stores operator == msg.sender instead, so for some fuzzed x (x != owner) the stored operator differs from the argument and the property is violated.

For any owner caller and any address arg, calling setOperator(_operator) results in c.operator() equaling the provided _operator in the reference; the mutant instead sets operator to msg.sender, so when the owner calls setOperator with an _operator different from the caller the stored operator will differ from the provided argument.

For any caller who is the owner and any address arg, calling setOperator(_operator) results in c.operator() equaling the provided _operator (reference); the mutant instead sets operator to msg.sender, so when the owner calls setOperator with an _operator != msg.sender the stored operator will differ — the test fuzzes the provided _operator and asserts c.operator() == _operator after the call.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any address arg _operator, calling setOperator(_operator) on the correct contract stores operator == _operator; the mutant instead stores operator == msg.sender, so there exist inputs (owner calling with _operator != owner) where the mutant's operator differs.

Invariant: only the contract owner can successfully call setOperator(address); the mutant removes this check allowing non-owners to change operator, so there exist caller addresses for which setOperator succeeds on the mutant but cannot on the reference.

For all caller addresses x, in the reference contract only the owner (deployer) can have setOperator succeed; the mutant permits some non-owner callers to succeed, so there exists an address x for which calling setOperator(x) reverts on the reference but would succeed on the mutant.

For any caller address and target operator address, on the reference contract only the deployer (owner) can successfully call setOperator; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so there exist non-owner callers for which setOperator succeeds on the mutant but would revert on the reference.

For every caller address, when a non-owner calls setOperator on the reference contract it must revert (only the owner can change operator); the mutant removes the owner check so there exist caller addresses for which setOperator succeeds on the mutant but reverts on the reference.

For any caller A and target operator addr, in the reference contract only the owner (deployer) can successfully execute setOperator(addr) (non-owners' attempts revert); the mutant removes this restriction so there exist non-owner callers for which setOperator(addr) succeeds — the property is that setOperator only succeeds when called by the owner.

Calling setRewardsRecipient(x) always updates the public rewardsRecipient to x (for all x) in the reference; the mutant that comments out the assignment breaks this because rewardsRecipient remains unchanged for some x.

For every caller and address argument, after calling setRewardsRecipient(addr) on the correct contract, the public rewardsRecipient getter returns addr; the mutant that comments out the assignment violates this (there exist inputs where rewardsRecipient is not updated).

For any address newRecipient and any caller who is the owner, calling setRewardsRecipient(newRecipient) causes C.rewardsRecipient() to equal newRecipient; the mutant that comments out the assignment violates this because after the call the stored rewardsRecipient may remain the old value for some newRecipient inputs.

For every address x and when called by the contract owner, setRewardsRecipient(x) sets the public rewardsRecipient to x; the mutant that comments out the assignment violates this because after the call rewardsRecipient may remain different (not equal to x) for some x.

For every address newRecipient and when called by the contract owner, calling setRewardsRecipient(newRecipient) on the correct contract makes c.rewardsRecipient() equal newRecipient (the mutant that comments out the assignment breaks this for some newRecipient values), so the property asserts equality after the call.

For any input address X, after calling setRewardsRecipient(X) the contract's public rewardsRecipient equals the passed-in X (reference); the mutant instead stores address(0) and thus violates this for any X != address(0).

For any caller and any nonzero input address addr, after calling setRewardsRecipient(addr) the contract's public rewardsRecipient equals addr (the mutant instead always stores address(0), causing a mismatch for any addr != address(0)).

For any fuzzed nonzero address `addr`, after the owner calls setRewardsRecipient(addr) the contract's public rewardsRecipient equals the passed-in addr (the mutant instead stores address(0), so this property will fail for some nonzero addr inputs).

For every address x, when the owner calls setRewardsRecipient(x) the contract's public rewardsRecipient becomes x; the mutant instead sets rewardsRecipient to address(0) causing a mismatch for any x != address(0).

For any address a passed to setRewardsRecipient by the owner, the contract's public rewardsRecipient equals the passed-in address; the mutant instead stores address(0) and thus violates this for any non-zero address input.

For any caller address X passed as the _recipeint parameter to setRewardsRecipient, the correct contract stores that exact address in rewardsRecipient; the mutant instead stores msg.sender (caller), so when the caller is different from the passed-in _recipeint the mutant's stored value differs and the property is violated.

For any caller and any address parameter, the correct contract stores the provided _recipeint as rewardsRecipient after setRewardsRecipient is called; the mutant instead stores msg.sender, so when the owner calls setRewardsRecipient with a different address the stored rewardsRecipient will differ and the property is violated.

For any address X that the owner passes to setRewardsRecipient(X), the contract's rewardsRecipient getter returns that same address after the call; the mutant instead stores msg.sender and so will differ when owner != X.

For any owner caller and any address param, after setRewardsRecipient(_recipeint) completes the contract's rewardsRecipient getter equals the provided _recipeint; the mutant assigns msg.sender instead, so when owner != _recipeint the mutant's stored value differs.

For every call to setRewardsRecipient by the owner with any address argument X, the correct contract stores rewardsRecipient == X after the call; the mutant stores msg.sender instead, so when the owner passes an X != owner the mutant's rewardsRecipient != X and the property is violated.

For every pool id, the correct contract's isCvxShutdown() returns booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown (i.e. true exactly when the booster reports shutdown); the mutant inverts that boolean, so there exists some pId where returned value differs.

For any pool id, the correct contract's isCvxShutdown() returns the booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown value; the mutant flips that boolean (returns !shutdown) so for any pId where booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown differs from its negation (i.e. either true or false) the mutant will return a different result — the rule: isCvxShutdown() == booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown for all inputs, which the mutant violates for some pId.

For every pool id stored in cvxPoolInfo, C.isCvxShutdown() returns the booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown value; the mutant inverts that boolean (returns !shutdown) and thus will disagree for at least one poolInfo.shutdown value.

For all pool ids stored in c (cvxPoolInfo.pId), C.isCvxShutdown() returns exactly the boolean reported by booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown; the mutant negates that boolean, so there exist pool ids where the mutant's return differs.
For every cvxPoolInfo.pId value, C.isCvxShutdown() returns exactly the booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown boolean; the mutant negates that boolean, so for some pId the mutant's return will differ.

For every possible pool id stored in c.cvxPoolInfo.pId, the real contract returns booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown when calling isCvxShutdown(); the mutant always returns true, so there exist pId values for which the real contract's return (which depends on the external booster) is different from true and thus the mutant breaks the rule.

For every pool id value, the reference contract's isCvxShutdown() returns the shutdown flag provided by the configured booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown (so it can be false for some pId), whereas the mutant always returns true, thus violating the rule whenever the real booster would report shutdown == false.

For every pool id input, the reference C returns whatever the configured booster's poolInfo(pId).shutdown is (which can be false), whereas the mutant always returns true — so there exists some booster behavior (shutdown == false) for which the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For every pool id configured in C, isCvxShutdown() must return the shutdown flag reported by its booster.poolInfo(pId).shutdown (i.e. can be false for some booster implementations), but the mutant always returns true so it violates the rule whenever the booster would report shutdown == false.
